newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU foreign ministers wait for French EMU stance.
newsitem.headline: EU foreign ministers wait for French EMU stance.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers reacted cautiously on Monday to news of the French Socialists' sweeping victory in Sunday's elections and what this might mean for economic and monetary union (EMU).

"It's too early to say," British Foreign Minister Robin Cook said as he arrived for a routine ministerial meeting that was to discuss the draft treaty to be agreed at the EU's Amsterdam summit in two weeks.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the election of the Socialists marked an important change but that the rest of the EU would have to wait to see what it meant for Paris's European policy.
The French Socialists have said they are committed to monetary union, but with conditions, including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.

They want Italy and Spain to be in the first wave of countries to adopt the single currency from 1999 and have made clear they are unwilling to continue the fiscal austerity policy conducted by the outgoing government to qualify France for EMU.

Although this -- and a crisis over proposed German accounting methods -- have led to renewed discussion of a delay in EMU, most ministers played down any negative impact of the left's triumph on the treaty review or the timetable for EMU.
"It depends who will be foreign minister," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo told reporters on arrival. The Netherlands currently holds the rotating EU presidency.
Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Helm-Wallens, welcoming the election of another Socialist government, said it was important to stick to the timetable for EMU.
European Commission President Jacques Santer, whose executive is charged with ensuring that the Maastricht treaty is complied with, also said the current timetable had to be met.
Britain's Cook refused to be drawn on whether a delay in EMU was now likely.
He said that as Britain was unlikely to join in the first wave, it was not for London to comment. "It's a matter for the French government and the German government to comment," he said.
